name: Ardhanareeswarar Temple, Tiruchengode (Thirukkodimadachengundrur)
deity: Shiva as Ardhanareeswarar, half Shiva and half Parvati in one form (the goddess as Bhagampiriyal)
period: A hilltop Paadal Petra Sthalam of Kongu Nadu, sung by Sambandar in the Tevaram (7th century)
summary: On the red hill of Tiruchengode, Shiva and Parvati are worshipped as one — Ardhanareeswarar, the Lord who is half the Goddess — in the Thirukkodimadachengundrur that Sambandar sang.

sections.history: Tiruchengode, in Namakkal district, takes its name from the red hill that rises at the edge of the town: Sengodu, the red peak. On its summit stands the temple the Tevaram calls Thirukkodimadachengundrur, the red hill of lofty mansions with flags. Sambandar sang it, and tradition says his hymn on the blue-throated Lord, the Thiruneelakanta pathigam, was sung here to free his companions from a fever of the Kongu country. It is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and one of the seven of Kongu Nadu. Arunagirinathar later praised the Murugan of this hill in the Tiruppugazh.
sections.architecture: Pilgrims climb some twelve hundred steps up the hill, passing a chain of rest mandapams on the way, though a ghat road now also reaches the top. Along the steps a great serpent some sixty feet long is carved into the rock and painted red, and the hill is also known as Nagagiri, the serpent mount. On the summit the old walls and pillared mandapams enclose the sanctum of Ardhanareeswarar and the shrine of Sengottu Velavar, Murugan of the red hill.
sections.legends: Tradition tells that Parvati performed a long penance, the Kedara Gowri vow, so that she might never be parted from her Lord, and Shiva granted her half of his own body; here he is worshipped in that united form, the right half Shiva and the left half the Goddess. A spring is said to rise at the foot of the image. Another story makes the hill a fragment of Mount Meru, broken off in a contest between Vayu and the serpent Adisesha, and coloured red by the serpent's blood.
sections.festivals: The great festival is the Vaikasi Visakam car festival in May–June, also called the Sengottu Velavar car festival, when Murugan rides out with Ardhanareeswarar and the goddess through the town below the hill. Maha Shivaratri, Kedara Gowri vratam at Deepavali time and the monthly Pradosham are also observed; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: The climb is part of the worship, and many make it at dawn, pausing at the mandapams and the carved serpent while the plain of Kongu opens out below. At the top, devotees stand before the rare image in which Shiva and Shakti are one, then visit Sengottu Velavar on the same summit. Married couples in particular come here to pray for harmony.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions; the hilltop shrine may close at midday. Allow time for the climb, and confirm current timings and road access locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside the shrines. Comfortable clothing suits the climb. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctums; the views and the carved serpent on the steps may be photographed, but ask the temple staff before taking pictures of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruchengode lies about 20 km north-east of Erode and about 45 km south-west of Salem, with frequent buses from both. Erode Junction is the nearest major railway station; Coimbatore International Airport is the nearest large airport, with Salem's smaller airport also in reach. The hilltop is reached by the steps or by the ghat road.
